chapter.title: Performance and Core Web Vitals
chapter.summary: How LCP, INP and CLS are really measured, how to shorten the loading critical path, and how to keep the main thread free at runtime, with the DevTools workflow to prove each fix.

lessons.title: Core Web Vitals: LCP, INP and CLS in depth
lessons.summary: Exact definitions and thresholds, how browsers compute LCP, INP and CLS, the field vs lab gap, CrUX and RUM, a fix playbook per sub-part, bfcache, and how to guard metrics.

parts.label: How they are measured
parts.body:
## Why these three metrics

Older performance metrics measured browser milestones (`DOMContentLoaded`, `load`) that users never see. Google's **Core Web Vitals** program picked three metrics that each answer one question a user actually asks:

| Question | Metric | Good | Poor |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Is the main content here yet?" | **LCP**, Largest Contentful Paint | <= 2.5 s | > 4.0 s |
| "Does the page respond when I interact?" | **INP**, Interaction to Next Paint | <= 200 ms | > 500 ms |
| "Is the page jumping around?" | **CLS**, Cumulative Layout Shift | <= 0.1 | > 0.25 |

Values between "good" and "poor" are "needs improvement". The assessment is made at the **75th percentile (p75)** of real page views, separately for mobile and desktop. p75 is a deliberate choice: the median would hide the slow quarter of your users, while p95 or p99 would be dominated by outliers you cannot control (a train going into a tunnel). A page passes when all three metrics are good at p75.

Two supporting metrics are not "core" but are essential for diagnosis: **TTFB** (Time to First Byte, good <= 0.8 s) and **FCP** (First Contentful Paint, good <= 1.8 s). A slow TTFB caps how good LCP can be.

INP replaced **FID** (First Input Delay) as a Core Web Vital in March 2024. FID only measured the delay before the *first* interaction's handler started; it ignored handler time, rendering time, and every later interaction. Most sites passed FID while still feeling sluggish. INP fixed that by measuring the full latency of all interactions.

## LCP: how the browser decides

**What counts as a candidate:** `img` elements (the first frame for animated images), `image` elements inside SVG, `video` elements (poster image or first displayed frame), elements with a background image loaded through CSS `url()`, and block-level elements containing text nodes.

**How it is measured, step by step:**

1. As the page renders, every time a new largest candidate is painted, the browser emits a `largest-contentful-paint` performance entry with its render time, size and element.
2. Size is the area visible **inside the viewport**. Parts clipped or off-screen do not count. For images, the browser uses the smaller of the displayed size and the intrinsic size, so upscaling a tiny image does not make it "large". Margins, padding and borders do not count.
3. The LCP element can change during load: first a heading paints, then a hero image that is bigger, so the image becomes the new LCP.
4. The browser **stops reporting new candidates once the user interacts** (tap, click, key press, scroll), because content appearing after that is likely a response to the user.
5. The final LCP is the last entry before that point or before the page is hidden.

Refinements Chrome applies: elements with `opacity: 0` are not candidates; images that are mostly blank or low-information (placeholders) are ignored; an element removed from the DOM still counts if it was the largest when painted. If a page is opened in a background tab, its LCP is not meaningful and RUM libraries discard it.

**The four sub-parts** (from web.dev's "Optimize LCP") turn one number into a diagnosis:

```text
| TTFB | resource load delay | resource load duration | element render delay |
  server  time until the LCP     downloading the LCP      time from resource loaded
  + net   resource starts loading  resource itself          to pixels on screen
```

For text LCP there is no resource, so it is TTFB plus render delay (often waiting for a web font or render-blocking CSS). web.dev's guidance is that load delay and render delay should be close to zero; when they are large, the problem is discovery and blocking, not bandwidth.

## INP: how it is computed

INP is built on the **Event Timing API**. For every discrete interaction (pointer down and up, click, tap, key press), the browser records:

```text
input event timestamp
 |--- input delay ---|--- processing time ---|--- presentation delay ---|
 (main thread busy)   (all event listeners for   (style, layout, paint of the
                      pointerdown/up/click or    next frame after handlers)
                      keydown/keyup)
                                                                         ^ next frame presented
```

- Events belonging to the same user gesture (for a tap: `pointerdown`, `pointerup`, `click`) share an `interactionId`, and the interaction's latency is the **longest duration** among them.
- Durations are rounded to 8 ms granularity.
- **Hover and scroll are not interactions** for INP. Scroll smoothness is a separate problem (and usually compositor-driven).
- The page's INP is the **worst interaction latency** of the visit, except that for pages with many interactions one outlier is ignored for every 50 interactions. In practice that is close to the 98th percentile of interactions for long-lived pages.
- As with all Core Web Vitals, the site's reported INP is the p75 of those per-page-view values.

Because INP covers the whole visit, a single-page app that is fast on load but slow when filtering a table after two minutes still gets a poor INP. That is the point.

## CLS: how shifts are scored

A **layout shift** happens when a visible element changes its start position between two frames, without the user having caused it. Each shift gets a score:

```text
layout shift score = impact fraction x distance fraction

impact fraction:   area of the viewport affected by unstable elements
                   (union of their before and after positions) / viewport area
distance fraction: greatest distance any unstable element moved / largest viewport dimension
```

Example: a banner pushes an article down by 25% of the viewport height, and the article (before plus after positions) covers 75% of the viewport. Score = 0.75 x 0.25 = 0.1875. One such shift alone is "needs improvement".

Shifts are grouped into **session windows**: a window collects consecutive shifts less than 1 second apart, up to a maximum of 5 seconds. CLS is the score of the **largest session window**, not the sum over the whole visit. That change (made in 2021) stopped long-lived pages from accumulating unbounded CLS.

What does **not** count:

- Shifts within **500 ms after a discrete user input** (the entry carries `hadRecentInput: true`), so expanding an accordion on click is fine.
- Animations of `transform`, which do not change layout position.
- New elements appearing without moving existing ones.

## Field measurement: the APIs underneath

All three are exposed through `PerformanceObserver` in Chromium:

| Metric | Entry type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| LCP | `largest-contentful-paint` | Use `buffered: true` to receive entries that happened before your script loaded |
| INP | `event` (with `durationThreshold`) plus `first-input` | Group by `interactionId`; minimum threshold 16 ms |
| CLS | `layout-shift` | Skip entries with `hadRecentInput`; compute session windows |

You should almost never reimplement this. Google's `web-vitals` library (a few KB) handles the edge cases: page visibility changes, back/forward cache restores (which start a new measurement), prerendered pages (measured from activation), and reporting the final value when the page is hidden. Its attribution build adds the diagnostic detail: the LCP element and sub-part timings, the INP target selector and phase breakdown, and the largest shifting element.

**Browser support caveat:** Chromium has supported these APIs for years, and other engines have been adding LCP and Event Timing more recently. Chrome's public dataset, **CrUX**, only contains data from opted-in Chrome users. Check current support before assuming your RUM numbers represent Safari or Firefox users.

**Single-page apps:** Core Web Vitals are measured per page load. Client-side route changes do not start a new LCP, and CLS and INP accumulate across the whole SPA session. Chrome has been experimenting with soft-navigation measurement, but as of this writing your RUM should also tag interactions with the current route so you can attribute slow INP to the right screen.

parts.label: Field vs lab and fixes
parts.body:
## Field data vs lab data

**Field data** (real-user monitoring, RUM) is what real users experienced on their devices, networks and cache states. **Lab data** is a controlled run on one simulated device. web.dev's "Why lab and field data can be different" is worth reading in full; the summary is that they answer different questions and you need both.

| | Field | Lab |
|---|---|---|
| Sources | CrUX (Chrome UX Report), PageSpeed Insights field section, Search Console Core Web Vitals report, your own RUM with `web-vitals` | Lighthouse, Chrome DevTools Performance panel, WebPageTest, Lighthouse CI |
| Measures INP? | Yes, real interactions | Only if you script interactions; a plain Lighthouse load uses Total Blocking Time (TBT) as a proxy |
| Freshness | CrUX is a 28-day rolling window (API updated daily, BigQuery monthly) | Instant |
| Diagnostic detail | Limited unless you send attribution | Full traces, waterfalls, call stacks |
| Good for | "Which pages and metrics are bad, for whom?" and proving a fix worked | "Why is it bad?" and catching regressions before release |

**Why they disagree**, the reasons you should be able to list:

1. **Device and network.** Lighthouse mobile emulates a mid-range phone with throttled CPU and network; your users may be faster (a desktop-heavy B2B app) or much slower (entry-level Android in emerging markets).
2. **Cache state.** Lab runs are usually cold. Real repeat visitors have cached assets, a warm connection, maybe a service worker; first-time visitors from search do not.
3. **The LCP element differs.** Viewport size, logged-in state, cookie banners, A/B variants and personalisation change what the largest element is.
4. **Interactions.** Lighthouse does not tap anything during a navigation run. Real users tap during hydration, open menus, type into filters after minutes on the page.
5. **Page lifetime.** CLS and INP accumulate over the visit. A lab load lasts seconds; a real session may last half an hour with infinite scroll and lazy-loaded ads.
6. **Back/forward cache and prerendering.** Pages restored from the bfcache or activated from a prerender have near-instant LCP in the field and never appear like that in the lab.
7. **Third parties.** Tag managers can inject scripts in production that are not present on staging.

The workflow: **field data finds the problem, lab data explains it, field data confirms the fix.** Do not chase a Lighthouse score that already looks fine while field INP is poor.

### Getting CrUX data

- **PageSpeed Insights** shows URL-level and origin-level field data when there is enough traffic, plus a Lighthouse lab run.
- **Search Console** groups similar URLs (templates) and flags those failing each metric, which is useful for prioritising.
- **CrUX API** returns p75 values and histograms per URL or origin, by form factor, for dashboards and alerting.
- **CrUX History API** gives weekly trends over months, which is how you see whether a fix moved the p75 after the window rolled over.
- Your **own RUM** fills the gaps: low-traffic pages, logged-in pages that CrUX cannot see publicly, non-Chrome browsers where supported, and route-level attribution in SPAs.

## The fix playbook per metric

web.dev's "The most effective ways to improve Core Web Vitals" ranks fixes by impact for typical sites. Here is a condensed playbook, organised by the sub-part that is bad.

### LCP

| Dominant sub-part | Typical cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| TTFB | Slow server render, uncached HTML, redirect chains, far-away origin | Cache HTML at a CDN (with `stale-while-revalidate`), stream the response, remove redirects, keep data near the render |
| Resource load delay | LCP image injected by JavaScript, set as a CSS background, or `loading="lazy"` | Put a real image element in server HTML; never lazy-load it; add `fetchpriority="high"`; preload backgrounds |
| Resource load duration | Oversized image, wrong format, competing downloads | Responsive `srcset` and `sizes`, AVIF or WebP, an image CDN; fewer competing high-priority requests |
| Element render delay | Render-blocking CSS or sync scripts, waiting for web fonts, client-side rendering, A/B scripts hiding the page | Inline critical CSS, defer scripts, `font-display`, server render, move experiments to the server or edge |

The single most common LCP bug in modern apps is the **late-discovered hero image**: a client-rendered React page whose image URL only exists after the bundle downloads, executes and fetches JSON. No amount of CDN tuning fixes that; the image must be discoverable in the initial HTML.

### INP

| Dominant phase | Typical cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Input delay | Long tasks already running when the user taps: hydration, large bundles evaluating, third-party tags, timers | Split and defer JavaScript, reduce hydration (Server Components, islands), delay non-essential tags, yield in long work |
| Processing time | Event handlers doing too much synchronously: large state updates, re-rendering big trees, synchronous storage or analytics | Do the visual update first and defer the rest (`scheduler.yield`, `requestAnimationFrame` plus `setTimeout`), transitions, memoisation, virtualise, Web Workers |
| Presentation delay | Large DOM updates, expensive style and layout, layout thrashing, huge DOM size | Smaller DOM, `content-visibility: auto`, avoid forced synchronous layout, CSS containment |

A useful habit: **give visual feedback first.** If a click must save data and recompute a summary, update the button's pressed state, yield so the frame paints, then do the rest. INP measures until the next paint, so making that paint happen quickly is the goal, as long as the feedback is meaningful.

### CLS

| Cause | Fix |
|---|---|
| Images, videos and iframes without dimensions | `width` and `height` attributes or CSS `aspect-ratio`; modern browsers reserve space from them |
| Ads, embeds and banners injected above content | Reserve a slot of the expected size; place late-loading content below the fold or in overlays |
| Web fonts swapping with different metrics | `font-display: optional` or metric-matched fallbacks (`size-adjust`, `ascent-override`); preload the critical font |
| Content inserted after load (consent banners, "new posts" bars) | Overlay instead of pushing content; insert only in response to user input |
| Skeletons that do not match final size | Make placeholders the same dimensions as content |
| Animating `top`, `left`, `height` | Animate `transform` instead |

A trick for diagnosing CLS in the lab: the DevTools Performance panel's "Layout shifts" track shows which nodes moved and by how much, and the Rendering tab can flash shifted regions as you scroll through the page.

## bfcache: the free win

The back/forward cache keeps a complete snapshot of a page in memory when the user navigates away, so going back restores it instantly with all JavaScript state. Those restores produce near-perfect field metrics. web.dev's bfcache article cites Chrome data showing roughly 1 in 10 desktop navigations and 1 in 5 mobile navigations are back or forward, so being eligible matters.

Common reasons a page is **not** eligible: `unload` event listeners (use `pagehide` instead), and in some browsers `Cache-Control: no-store` on the HTML; open connections and certain APIs can also block it. Chrome DevTools has a "Back/forward cache" test in the Application panel that lists the blocking reasons for the current page.

## Setting targets and guarding them

- **Set targets per template** (home, product, search, checkout), at p75 on mobile, because one site-wide number hides the page that is actually bad.
- **Alert on field regressions** from your RUM data, segmented by device and route, with enough volume to be meaningful.
- **Guard in CI** with lab metrics that correlate with the field: LCP and TBT from Lighthouse CI on a production build, bundle size budgets per route, and scripted interaction tests for critical flows.
- **Treat third-party tags as code**, with owners and reviews, because they are a top source of INP regressions that never touched your repository.

  B -->|"LCP"| L["Attribution: which sub-part dominates?"]
  B -->|"INP"| I["Attribution: target element and phase"]

parts.label: Interview
parts.body:
## What interviewers are really testing

Core Web Vitals questions are partly recall (names, thresholds, what replaced FID) and mostly method: can you explain how each metric is actually measured, why field and lab disagree, and how you would move a failing metric? Interviewers love follow-ups that expose shallow knowledge: "why p75?", "what does not count as a layout shift?", "how is INP different from TBT?". Answer with the measurement model, then the fix tied to a sub-part.

## Question 1: "Name the Core Web Vitals and their thresholds."

**Model answer:** LCP, INP and CLS, each judged at the 75th percentile of real page views, separately for mobile and desktop. Good LCP is 2.5 seconds or less, poor is over 4. Good INP is 200 milliseconds or less, poor is over 500. Good CLS is 0.1 or less, poor is over 0.25. INP replaced First Input Delay in March 2024 because FID only measured the delay before the first interaction's handler, not the handler or the rendering, and not later interactions.

## Question 2: "Walk me through how INP is measured."

**Model answer:**

> The browser's Event Timing API records each discrete interaction: clicks, taps and key presses, not hover or scroll. For each one it measures from the input timestamp until the next frame is presented, which covers three phases: input delay while the main thread is busy, processing time in all the event listeners, and presentation delay for style, layout and paint. Events from the same gesture share an interaction id, and the slowest event defines that interaction. The page's INP is roughly its worst interaction, ignoring one outlier per 50 interactions on busy pages, and the site's INP is the p75 across page views. In the lab, a plain Lighthouse run cannot measure it because nobody interacts, so it uses Total Blocking Time as a proxy.

## Question 3: "Why does the LCP element sometimes change, and when does measurement stop?"

**Model answer:** The browser emits a new LCP entry whenever a larger candidate paints: first a heading, then a hero image. It considers images, video posters, CSS background images and text blocks, sized by their visible area in the viewport, and for images capped at their intrinsic size. It stops looking once the user interacts by tapping, clicking, scrolling or pressing a key, because later content is likely a response to them. So the reported LCP is the last candidate before the first input or before the page is hidden.

## Question 4: "How is CLS calculated? Does a long session accumulate a huge CLS?"

**Model answer:** Each unexpected shift scores impact fraction times distance fraction: the share of the viewport affected by moving elements times how far they moved relative to the viewport. Shifts within 500 ms of user input are excluded, and transform animations do not count. Shifts are grouped into session windows of up to 5 seconds where consecutive shifts are less than a second apart, and CLS is the largest window, not the sum. So a long session does not accumulate unbounded CLS, but one bad burst, such as ads loading together, defines the score.

## Question 5: "Our Lighthouse score is 95, but Search Console says our product pages fail INP. Explain and fix."

**Model answer:**

1. **Explain the gap:** Lighthouse is a single cold load on an emulated device with no interaction. Field INP comes from real users on real devices tapping during hydration, with production third-party tags, over long sessions.
2. **Find the interaction:** add RUM with `web-vitals` attribution to get the INP target selector and the phase breakdown per template. Long Animation Frame data tells me which scripts were running.
3. **Fix by phase:** if input delay dominates, the main thread is busy when users tap, so I reduce and defer JavaScript, cut hydration, and delay tags. If processing dominates, the handler does too much, so I paint feedback first and defer or yield the rest, use transitions, memoise or virtualise. If presentation delay dominates, the DOM update is too big, so I shrink it.
4. **Verify:** reproduce in the Performance panel with CPU throttling, then watch RUM p75 and wait for the CrUX 28-day window to roll over.

## Question 6: "Why p75 and not the average?"

**Model answer:** Averages hide distribution: a few very fast loads can mask a slow quarter of users, and a few extreme outliers can drag the mean. The median would ignore half the users' worse experiences. p75 means three out of four page views meet the target, which captures most slow-device and slow-network users without being dominated by outliers you cannot control.

## Question 7: "How do Core Web Vitals work in a single-page app?"

**Model answer:** They are measured per document load. LCP happens once on the initial load; client-side route changes do not produce new LCPs. INP and CLS accumulate across the whole SPA session, so a slow screen deep in the app affects the page's INP. Chrome has experimented with soft-navigation measurement, but in practice I tag RUM events with the current route so I can attribute slow interactions to a screen, and I watch custom metrics for route transitions.

## Quick-fire follow-ups

| Follow-up | Strong short answer |
|---|---|
| "What is a good TTFB and FCP?" | TTFB <= 0.8 s, FCP <= 1.8 s; supporting metrics, not core |
| "Does lazy-loading the hero help LCP?" | No, it delays discovery; use `fetchpriority="high"` and no lazy loading |
| "Does an accordion opening on click hurt CLS?" | No, shifts within 500 ms of input are excluded |
| "Does scrolling count for INP?" | No, only discrete interactions such as click, tap and key press |
| "Where does CrUX data come from?" | Opted-in Chrome users, 28-day rolling window, URL and origin level |
| "What is the bfcache's effect on metrics?" | Restored pages are near-instant; `unload` listeners can make pages ineligible |
| "TBT vs INP?" | TBT sums long-task time beyond 50 ms during load in the lab; INP measures real interaction latency over the visit |

## Common mistakes

- Quoting FID as a current Core Web Vital, or old thresholds.
- Saying CLS is the sum of all shifts over the visit.
- Treating Lighthouse scores as the goal instead of field p75.
- Optimising image bytes when the real LCP problem is late discovery.
- Forgetting that INP includes rendering after handlers, not just handler time.
- Ignoring third-party tags and the tag manager in INP investigations.

keyPoints: Core Web Vitals are LCP, INP and CLS judged at p75 of real page views per device type; INP replaced FID in March 2024.
LCP is the last largest-candidate paint before the first input, sized by visible area; split it into TTFB, load delay, load duration and render delay.
INP uses Event Timing: input delay plus processing plus presentation for clicks, taps and keys, taking roughly the worst interaction of the visit.
CLS is the largest session window of unexpected shifts, each scored impact fraction times distance fraction; shifts within 500 ms of input are excluded.
Field data finds the problem and confirms fixes; lab data explains it. Lighthouse loads do not interact and use TBT as a proxy for INP.
Use web-vitals with attribution for RUM; tag routes in SPAs because LCP happens once and INP and CLS span the session.
bfcache eligibility (no unload listeners) gives near-instant back and forward navigations for free.

check.q: A tap triggers pointerdown (40 ms), pointerup (30 ms) and click (180 ms) events, each measured to the next paint. What latency does INP record for this interaction?
options: 250 ms, the sum
180 ms, the longest event in the interaction
40 ms, the first event
83 ms, the average
check.why: Events from one gesture share an interactionId and the interaction's latency is the longest duration among them, here the click.

check.q: A user clicks Show more and content expands 200 ms later, pushing the footer down. How does this affect CLS?
options: It adds the full shift score to CLS
It doubles the score because it happened after load
It counts only on mobile
It is excluded because it happened within 500 ms of a discrete user input
check.why: Layout shifts within 500 ms after user input carry hadRecentInput and are excluded, because the user expects the page to change in response to their action.

check.q: Why can a page have a near-perfect lab Lighthouse result and still fail INP in CrUX?
options: CrUX measures INP on desktop only
Lighthouse measures INP on a faster CPU
A Lighthouse navigation run does not interact with the page, while real users tap during hydration on slower devices with production tags
INP is only measured after 28 days
check.why: INP requires real interactions. A plain Lighthouse load reports TBT as a proxy; real devices, timing of taps, long sessions and third-party scripts create the field gap.

lessons.title: Loading performance: critical path to cache
lessons.summary: The critical rendering path in round trips, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, compression, Early Hints, resource hints and fetch priority, images, fonts, JavaScript splitting, caching layers and speculative loading.

parts.label: Critical path and network
parts.body:
## The core idea

Loading performance is about one thing: **getting the bytes that matter for the first meaningful screen to the browser as early as possible, and getting everything else out of their way.** Total page weight matters less than people think. What matters is the **critical path**: the chain of dependent requests and processing steps that must complete before the user sees the main content. A 3 MB page can render its hero in 1 second if the critical path is short; a 300 KB page can take 5 seconds if its hero image is discovered only after three sequential round trips.

An analogy: boarding a plane. It does not matter how much luggage is in the hold; what matters is whether the passengers in row 1 can sit down without waiting for everyone behind them.

## The critical rendering path, step by step

```text
1. DNS lookup            (often cached; 20-120 ms cold)
2. TCP + TLS handshake   (TLS 1.3: 1 RTT after TCP; QUIC combines both: 1 RTT, 0-RTT on resumption)
3. Request HTML          -> server think time -> first byte (TTFB)
4. Parse HTML (streaming), preload scanner discovers CSS, JS, images, fonts
5. CSS downloaded and parsed -> CSSOM (render-blocking)
6. Sync scripts in <head> block parsing until fetched and executed
7. Style + layout + paint -> First Contentful Paint
8. LCP resource (image or font) fetched -> LCP
```

The **critical resources** are those that block the first render: the HTML, render-blocking CSS, and parser-blocking scripts. Each one costs at least one round trip, and dependencies chain: CSS that `@import`s another CSS file, a font referenced only from CSS, or an image URL that only exists after JavaScript runs. web.dev's "Understand the critical path" explains that minimising the number of critical resources, their bytes, and the **length of the dependency chain** (the number of sequential round trips) is the whole game.

Round-trip time dominates on mobile. At 100 ms RTT, a chain of HTML, then CSS, then font, then text paint is at least three or four round trips beyond the connection setup, regardless of bandwidth.

## HTTP versions and what they change

| | HTTP/1.1 | HTTP/2 | HTTP/3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Transport | TCP | TCP | QUIC over UDP |
| Requests per connection | One at a time (browsers open about 6 connections per origin) | Many multiplexed streams | Many multiplexed streams |
| Head-of-line blocking | Per connection, at the HTTP level | Fixed at HTTP level, but a lost TCP packet stalls all streams | Per stream only; loss on one stream does not stall others |
| Header compression | None | HPACK | QPACK |
| Handshake | TCP + TLS | TCP + TLS | Combined, 1 RTT, 0-RTT resumption |
| Connection migration | No | No | Yes (survives Wi-Fi to mobile switch) |

Practical consequences:

- **HTTP/1.1-era hacks hurt on HTTP/2+.** Domain sharding (spreading assets across `static1`, `static2` hostnames) adds DNS and TLS handshakes and breaks prioritisation. Giant concatenated bundles and sprite sheets reduce cache granularity. With multiplexing, many smaller, separately cacheable files are fine, within reason (each request still has overhead, and compression works better on larger files).
- **HTTP/2 Server Push is gone.** Chrome removed it in 2022 because it rarely helped and often pushed resources already in cache. Its replacements are `preload` and **103 Early Hints**: the server sends an interim `103` response with `Link: rel=preload` or `rel=preconnect` headers while it is still generating the HTML, so the browser can start fetching critical CSS and fonts during server think time.
- **HTTP/3** helps most on lossy mobile networks and for users far from the server. Most CDNs enable it with a toggle; browsers discover it via the `Alt-Svc` header or DNS HTTPS records.
- **0-RTT resumption** lets a returning client send the request with the first packet, but the data can be replayed by an attacker, so servers must accept only idempotent requests in 0-RTT.

**Compression:** serve text assets with Brotli (widely supported and usually smaller than gzip) and consider Zstandard, which Chromium-based browsers and Firefox now accept as a content encoding. Pre-compress static assets at build time at high levels; compress dynamic HTML on the fly at moderate levels, because high levels cost server CPU and TTFB.

## Resource hints and priorities

The browser assigns each request a priority based on its type and position (CSS in the head: highest; a script at the end of the body: lower; images: low until known to be in the viewport). Hints let you correct the browser when it cannot know what matters.

| Hint | What it does | Use for | Mistake |
|---|---|---|---|
| `rel="preconnect"` | DNS + TCP + TLS to an origin now | 1 to 3 critical third-party origins (image CDN, font host, API) | Preconnecting to 10 origins; unused connections are closed after about 10 s |
| `rel="dns-prefetch"` | DNS only | Many less-critical origins; fallback for preconnect | None really, cheap |
| `rel="preload"` | Fetch this resource now at its type's priority | Late-discovered critical resources: a font referenced in CSS, a background hero image, a critical script loaded by another script | Preloading too much competes with the real critical resources; preloading something unused wastes bandwidth and triggers a console warning |
| `rel="modulepreload"` | Fetch and parse an ES module and its graph | Critical JS module dependencies | Same as preload |
| `rel="prefetch"` | Low-priority fetch for a future navigation | The next page's bundle | Prefetching on slow or metered connections |
| `fetchpriority="high"` / `"low"` | Adjusts priority relative to the default | High: the LCP image. Low: below-the-fold carousel images, non-critical scripts | Marking many things high, which cancels out |

Two rules people miss:

1. **Fonts must be preloaded with `crossorigin`**, even from your own origin, because fonts are fetched in CORS mode. Without it, the preload is not reused and the font downloads twice.
2. **A preload in the HTML is only as early as the HTML.** If TTFB is 1.5 s, hints in the document are 1.5 s late; Early Hints or a faster server move them earlier.

web.dev's "Optimize resource loading with the Fetch Priority API" shows the canonical win: adding `fetchpriority="high"` to an LCP image that the browser would otherwise start at low priority, typically improving LCP noticeably on image-heavy pages.

## Speculative loading for the next navigation

The fastest navigation is one that already happened. Options, from lightest to heaviest:

- **Prefetch** the next page's resources (`<link rel="prefetch">` or framework link prefetching on hover or viewport).
- **Speculation Rules API** (Chromium): a JSON script that declares URLs or patterns to prefetch or **prerender**, with an `eagerness` setting (`immediate`, `eager`, `moderate` on hover, `conservative` on pointer down). A prerendered page is fully loaded in a hidden tab and activates instantly, giving near-zero LCP.
- **bfcache** for back and forward navigations.

Trade-offs: prerendering uses memory, CPU and bandwidth, and runs analytics and other scripts before the user arrives, so pages should check `document.prerendering` and the `prerenderingchange` event before counting views or doing side effects. Never speculate on URLs with side effects (log out, add to cart via GET).

parts.label: Assets and caching
parts.body: ## Images Images are the LCP element on most pages and the largest share of bytes on many. The rules, in order of impact: **1. Make the LCP image discoverable and prioritised.** It must be a real image element in the server HTML (not injected by JavaScript, not a CSS background unless preloaded), never `loading="lazy"`, and ideally `fetchpriority="high"`. **2. Serve the right size.** Use `srcset` with width descriptors and an accurate `sizes` attribute so the browser picks the smallest adequate file for the layout width and device pixel ratio: ```text ``` Without `sizes`, the browser assumes `100vw` and over-downloads for images that are actually half the page wide. MDN's "Responsive images" guide covers `srcset`, `sizes` and the `picture` element for art direction (a different crop on mobile). **3. Use modern formats.** AVIF and WebP are typically much smaller than JPEG at similar quality. Serve them through `picture` with a fallback, or let an image CDN negotiate via the `Accept` header (remember `Vary: Accept`). **4. Always reserve space.** `width` and `height` attributes (or CSS `aspect-ratio`) let the browser compute the box before the image arrives, preventing layout shift. **5. Lazy-load below the fold** with `loading="lazy"` (native, no JavaScript) and `decoding="async"`. Be careful with carousels and tabs: images visible on first paint should not be lazy. Framework components (`next/image`, Astro's `Image`) automate most of this; the remaining job is telling them which image is the LCP (`priority` or `preload`). ## Fonts Web fonts sit on the critical path for text: they are discovered only after CSS is parsed, and text may be invisible until they load. web.dev's "Best practices for fonts" recommends: - **Self-host** or use a framework font loader, avoiding a separate connection to a font provider. If you must use a third-party host, `preconnect` to it. - **Preload only the one or two critical font files** (with `crossorigin`), typically the regular weight used for body text and headings above the fold. - **Choose `font-display` deliberately:** `swap` shows fallback text immediately and swaps when the font arrives (good for FCP, can cause layout shift); `optional` gives the font a very short window and otherwise keeps the fallback for this page view (best for CLS; the font is cached for next time); `block` hides text, which you rarely want. - **Match fallback metrics** with `size-adjust`, `ascent-override`, `descent-override` and `line-gap-override` on a local fallback `@font-face`, so the swap barely moves anything. `next/font` and tools like Fontaine generate these. - **Subset** to the character ranges you use (`unicode-range`) and use WOFF2. Variable fonts can replace several static weights with one file, but check the size. ## JavaScript: ship less, later JavaScript is the most expensive byte: it must be downloaded, decompressed, parsed, compiled and executed, mostly on the main thread, and with SSR it also hydrates. It hurts LCP (bandwidth and render-blocking) and INP (main-thread time). | Technique | Mechanism | Notes | |---|---|---| | Route-level code splitting | Each route gets its own chunk | Default in modern frameworks; watch the shared chunk | | Component-level splitting | `import()`, `React.lazy`, `next/dynamic` | For heavy, below-the-fold or rarely used UI (charts, editors, maps) | | Interaction-driven loading | Load on click or hover (emoji picker, video player) | Prefetch on hover or idle to hide the delay | | Tree shaking | Bundler drops unused ES module exports | Needs ESM, side-effect-free modules (`"sideEffects": false`); barrel files can defeat it | | Server-side rendering of static parts | Server Components, islands | Code for non-interactive UI never ships | | Modern output | Target evergreen browsers, avoid unnecessary polyfills | Differential bundles are rarely needed now | | `defer` / `type="module"` | Do not block the parser | Avoid sync scripts in the head | Measure **first-load JavaScript per route** with a bundle analyser, and look for duplicated dependencies, whole libraries imported for one function, locale data, and icon sets. ## CSS CSS is render-blocking by design. Keep the CSS needed for the first screen small, inline it if it is tiny (frameworks do this), and load the rest without blocking. Avoid `@import` chains. Utility-first frameworks with purging (Tailwind) usually produce small CSS; CSS-in-JS libraries that inject styles at runtime add main-thread cost, which is why zero-runtime approaches became popular. ## Caching: the request you do not make ```text Request for /assets/app.3f9a1c.js -> memory cache / bfcache? (same document, back navigation) -> service worker? (if registered: cache-first, network-first, etc.) -> HTTP cache (disk)? fresh by max-age? -> use it, no request stale? -> conditional request with ETag / Last-Modified -> 304 or 200 -> CDN edge cache? (s-maxage, stale-while-revalidate) -> origin ``` | Resource | Header | Why | |---|---|---| | Hashed static assets (`app.3f9a1c.js`, fonts, images with hashed names) | `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable` | Content never changes for that URL; a new deploy gets a new URL | | HTML shared by all users | `Cache-Control: public, max-age=0, s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=600` | Browser revalidates, CDN serves fast and refreshes in the background | | Personalised HTML | `Cache-Control: private, no-cache` | Browser may store but must revalidate; CDN must not share it | | Sensitive responses | `Cache-Control: no-store` | Never stored | **The golden rule:** hash assets and cache them forever; never cache HTML forever, because the HTML is what points to the current asset hashes. Avoid changing chunk hashes when content did not change (stable chunk ids), or every deploy invalidates every user's cache. **Service workers** add a programmable cache for offline support and instant repeat loads, but they are easy to get wrong (stale apps that never update, double caching). Use a library such as Workbox and a clear update strategy. ## CDNs and the edge A CDN cuts round-trip time by terminating connections close to the user and serving cached content from the edge. To benefit: cache static assets at the edge (easy), cache shared HTML with short `s-maxage` plus `stale-while-revalidate` (big TTFB win), use tag-based purging for content that changes on events, and keep personalised data out of shared cache keys. ## A loading checklist for a product page 1. TTFB under 0.8 s at p75: cached or streamed HTML, no redirect chain. 2. Critical CSS small and not chained; no sync scripts in the head. 3. LCP image in HTML, `fetchpriority="high"`, responsive AVIF or WebP, dimensions set. 4. One or two fonts preloaded with `crossorigin`, metric-matched fallback. 5. First-load JavaScript under a budget per route; heavy widgets split and loaded on interaction. 6. Third-party scripts deferred, with facades for embeds. 7. Hashed assets immutable; HTML revalidated; HTTP/3 and Brotli enabled at the CDN. 8. Speculation rules or prefetch for the most likely next page; bfcache eligible.

parts.label: Interview
parts.body:
## What interviewers are really testing

Loading questions test whether you think in **round trips, dependency chains and priorities**, rather than reciting "minify and compress". A strong candidate can draw the critical path for a page, point at the step that is slow, and pick the right lever: server and CDN for TTFB, discovery and priority for the LCP resource, less JavaScript for render and hydration, caching for repeat visits. Expect a scenario question ("our landing page takes 5 seconds on 4G") and follow-ups on HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3, resource hints and cache headers.

## Question 1: "What is the critical rendering path and how do you shorten it?"

**Model answer:**

> It is the sequence of steps and dependent requests before the first meaningful paint: connect, fetch HTML, discover and fetch render-blocking CSS and any parser-blocking scripts, build the DOM and CSSOM, lay out and paint, then fetch the LCP image or font. Its cost is mostly the number of sequential round trips, not total bytes. I shorten it by reducing critical resources (inline small critical CSS, defer scripts), flattening chains (no CSS @import, preload fonts and late-discovered images), making the LCP resource discoverable in HTML with high fetch priority, and cutting TTFB with edge caching or streaming, plus Early Hints so critical fetches start during server think time.

## Question 2: "HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3: what changed and what does it mean for frontend builds?"

**Model answer:** HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over one TCP connection with header compression, which removed the need for domain sharding and aggressive concatenation; but a lost TCP packet still stalls every stream. HTTP/3 runs on QUIC over UDP, so loss only stalls the affected stream, handshakes combine transport and TLS in one round trip, and connections survive network changes, which helps mobile users most. For builds, it means many moderately sized, independently cacheable chunks are fine, sharding is harmful, and Server Push is dead, replaced by preload and 103 Early Hints.

## Question 3: "preload vs prefetch vs preconnect: when do you use each?"

**Model answer:** Preconnect opens DNS, TCP and TLS early to an origin I will definitely use soon, like an image CDN; I limit it to a couple of origins. Preload fetches a specific resource needed for the current page that the browser would discover late, such as a font referenced from CSS (with `crossorigin`) or a CSS background hero. Prefetch is a low-priority fetch for a likely next navigation. The common mistake is preloading too much, which competes with the truly critical resources; `fetchpriority` is often the better tool for adjusting priority of resources already in the HTML, like the LCP image.

## Question 4: "How would you set cache headers for a typical SPA or Next.js deploy?"

**Model answer:** Hashed static assets get `public, max-age=31536000, immutable`, because a new deploy changes their URLs. HTML never gets long caching, because it points at the current hashes: shared HTML can be `s-maxage` with `stale-while-revalidate` at the CDN and revalidated by browsers; personalised HTML is `private, no-cache`; sensitive responses `no-store`. I keep chunk hashes stable when content does not change, so a deploy does not invalidate everyone's cache, and use tag-based purging for content updates.

## Question 5: "Our marketing landing page has a 5-second LCP on 4G. Walk me through it."

**Model answer, structured:**

1. **Confirm and segment** in field data: mobile, which countries, which template. Get the LCP element and sub-parts from RUM attribution.
2. **TTFB** high? Cache the HTML at the CDN, remove redirects (http to https to www), enable HTTP/3, consider Early Hints.
3. **Load delay** high? The hero is probably injected by JavaScript, lazy-loaded, or a CSS background. Put it in the HTML, remove lazy loading, add `fetchpriority="high"`.
4. **Load duration** high? The image is oversized: responsive `srcset` and correct `sizes`, AVIF, image CDN.
5. **Render delay** high? Render-blocking CSS chains, sync A/B testing scripts in the head, or client-side rendering. Inline critical CSS, move experiments server-side, prerender the page.
6. **Fonts** if the LCP is text: preload the font with `crossorigin`, `font-display` with metric-matched fallback.
7. **Verify** with a throttled lab run and WebPageTest filmstrip, then watch field p75.

## Question 6: "When is code splitting harmful?"

**Model answer:** When it splits code needed for the first screen into separate requests discovered late, creating a waterfall (main chunk loads, then requests the hero component chunk). When chunks are so small that request overhead and worse compression outweigh the benefit. When lazy-loaded components above the fold show spinners and cause layout shift. And when chunk boundaries change every deploy, defeating caching. Split by route and by heavy, below-the-fold or on-interaction features, and prefetch likely-needed chunks on hover or idle.

## Quick-fire follow-ups

| Follow-up | Strong short answer |
|---|---|
| "Why preload fonts with crossorigin?" | Fonts are fetched in CORS mode; without it the preload is not reused and the font downloads twice |
| "What replaced HTTP/2 Server Push?" | `preload` links and 103 Early Hints |
| "Is 0-RTT safe?" | Only for idempotent requests, because early data can be replayed |
| "What does `immutable` do?" | Tells the browser not to revalidate even on reload while fresh |
| "Why not lazy-load everything?" | Lazy images above the fold delay LCP; lazy loading is for off-screen content |
| "What are speculation rules?" | A Chromium API to prefetch or prerender likely next pages with configurable eagerness |
| "Brotli vs gzip?" | Brotli is usually smaller for text; pre-compress static assets at high levels |

## Common mistakes

- Talking about total page size instead of the critical path and round trips.
- Adding `preload` for many resources, which demotes the ones that matter.
- Lazy-loading the hero image, or rendering it from JavaScript.
- Domain sharding or giant single bundles on HTTP/2.
- Caching HTML with long `max-age`, so users get stale asset references after a deploy.
- Forgetting `sizes` on responsive images, so phones download desktop files.

check.q: A self-hosted font is preloaded with <link rel="preload" as="font" href="/inter.woff2"> but DevTools shows it downloaded twice. Why?
options: Fonts cannot be preloaded
The preload is missing the crossorigin attribute, so it does not match the CORS-mode font request
The server sent no ETag
HTTP/2 always downloads fonts twice
check.why: Fonts are fetched in anonymous CORS mode even from the same origin. A preload without crossorigin uses a different mode, so the browser cannot reuse it and fetches the font again.

check.q: What is the main advantage of HTTP/3 over HTTP/2 on a lossy mobile network?
options: It allows more than 6 connections per origin
It supports Server Push
Packet loss only stalls the affected stream instead of every stream on the connection
It removes the need for TLS
check.why: HTTP/2 multiplexes over one TCP connection, so a lost packet blocks all streams until retransmitted. QUIC handles loss per stream, and also combines the transport and TLS handshakes.

check.q: Which Cache-Control value is right for app.3f9a1c.js, a content-hashed bundle?
options: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
no-store
private, no-cache
public, max-age=60
check.why: The URL changes whenever the content changes, so the file can be cached for a year without revalidation. Short or no caching wastes requests; HTML is what must stay fresh.

lessons.title: Runtime performance: main thread, memory and profiling
lessons.summary: Long tasks and frame budgets, yielding and scheduling APIs, rendering costs, Web Workers, list virtualisation, finding memory leaks, and reading Chrome DevTools traces to find the real hot spot.

parts.label: Main thread and scheduling
parts.body:
## The core idea

Once a page has loaded, performance is about the **main thread**. It runs your JavaScript, the framework, every third-party script, style calculation, layout, paint recording and most event dispatch, one task at a time. When a task runs long, nothing else on that list can happen: taps wait, animations stutter, typing lags. Runtime performance is the craft of keeping the main thread available: doing less work, doing it in small pieces, doing it at the right time, or doing it somewhere else.

Picture a single checkout lane in a shop. One customer with a full trolley (a 300 ms task) blocks everyone with one item (a tap that needs 10 ms). You can make the trolley smaller (less work), let people with one item go in between (yielding), or open another lane for bulk orders (a Web Worker).

## Tasks, frames and budgets

A quick recap of the event loop from the browser-internals lesson, focusing on what matters for runtime work:

```text
[task] -> [all microtasks] -> [maybe render: rAF callbacks, style, layout, paint] -> [next task] ...
```

- A frame at 60 Hz is due every 16.7 ms (8.3 ms at 120 Hz). If the main thread is inside a task when a frame is due, the frame is late.
- A **long task** is any task over **50 ms**. The number comes from the RAIL model: to respond to input within 100 ms, work must be split into chunks small enough that input arriving mid-chunk can still be handled in time.
- **Total Blocking Time (TBT)** in Lighthouse sums the part of each long task beyond 50 ms during load. It is a lab proxy for input delay.
- In the field, the **Long Animation Frames (LoAF) API** reports frames whose total work exceeded 50 ms, with `blockingDuration` and per-script attribution (source URL, function name, invoker such as an event listener or a timer). It replaced the older Long Tasks API for diagnosis because it shows *which script* caused a slow frame, including third-party scripts.

Keep in mind that a long task is not only your code. Style recalculation over a huge DOM, forced synchronous layout, and garbage collection pauses also land in the same tasks.

## Yielding: giving the browser a turn

If work cannot be avoided, break it into pieces and **yield** between them so the browser can process input and render. web.dev's "Optimize long tasks" walks through the options:

| Technique | How it yields | Caveat |
|---|---|---|
| `setTimeout(fn, 0)` | Schedules the rest as a new task at the back of the queue | Other tasks (including third-party) may run first; nested timers clamp to 4 ms after several levels |
| `scheduler.yield()` | Yields, then continues at the **front** of the queue with the same priority | Chromium has shipped it since 2024 and other engines are adding it; feature-detect and fall back |
| `scheduler.postTask(fn, { priority })` | Queues a task with `user-blocking`, `user-visible` or `background` priority | Supported in Chromium and Firefox; abortable via `TaskController` |
| `requestIdleCallback(fn, { timeout })` | Runs when the browser is idle | May never run on a busy page without a timeout; not for user-visible work |
| `requestAnimationFrame(fn)` | Runs just before the next render | For visual writes, not for heavy computation |
| `isInputPending()` | Checked whether input is waiting | Chromium-only and effectively superseded by `scheduler.yield()` |

A good default pattern is "yield after a time budget": process items until about 5 to 10 ms have passed, then `await` a yield, and continue. It adapts to fast and slow devices automatically.

### Visual feedback first, the rest later

For interactions, the most effective INP fix is often to **paint the response before doing the follow-up work**:

```ts
button.addEventListener('click', async () => {
  button.setAttribute('aria-pressed', 'true'); // visual update, cheap
  await yieldToMain();                         // let the frame paint
  saveToServer();                              // non-urgent
  sendAnalytics();                             // non-urgent
  recomputeSidebarStats();                     // non-urgent
});
```

INP ends at the next paint after the interaction, so moving non-visual work after a yield directly cuts processing time. Make sure the immediate feedback is meaningful, though: a button that looks pressed but whose result arrives 2 seconds later is still a bad experience, just not an INP problem.

## Rendering work on the main thread

JavaScript is not the only cost. Style, layout and paint scale with DOM size and with how much of the page you invalidate.

- **DOM size.** Lighthouse warns above roughly 1,400 elements. Every style recalc and layout touches more nodes, and memory grows. Virtualisation and pagination keep it bounded.
- **Forced synchronous layout (layout thrashing).** Reading geometry (`offsetHeight`, `getBoundingClientRect()`) after a DOM write forces layout immediately. In a loop it forces layout N times. Batch reads before writes, or use `ResizeObserver` and `IntersectionObserver` instead of polling.
- **Broad invalidation.** Toggling a class on `body` or changing a CSS custom property on `:root` can restyle the whole document. Scope changes to the smallest subtree.
- **CSS containment.** `contain: layout paint` (or `contain: strict` with known size) tells the browser that changes inside an element do not affect outside layout, limiting work.
- **`content-visibility: auto`** skips style, layout and paint for off-screen sections until they approach the viewport, with `contain-intrinsic-size` providing a placeholder size so the scrollbar does not jump. web.dev's "content-visibility" article shows large rendering-time reductions on long pages. It is supported across modern engines, but test find-in-page and anchor links on your content.
- **Compositor-only animations.** Animate `transform` and `opacity` so animations run on the compositor thread and stay smooth even when the main thread is busy.

## Moving work off the main thread

**Web Workers** run JavaScript on another thread with no DOM access. They are the right tool for CPU-heavy, self-contained work: parsing large JSON or CSV files, search indexing and fuzzy matching, diffing, image processing, syntax highlighting, encryption, data aggregation for charts.

Trade-offs:

- Data is copied with structured cloning when posted, which itself costs main-thread time for large objects. Transfer `ArrayBuffer`s (zero-copy) when possible, or keep the data in the worker and send only queries and results.
- The message-passing API is awkward; Comlink wraps it in async function calls.
- Workers do not help with DOM-bound work (rendering a huge list). For that, render less.
- `OffscreenCanvas` lets a worker draw to a canvas, useful for charts and visualisations.

**WebAssembly** can speed up specific compute kernels (codecs, physics, parsers), usually inside a worker. It is not a general fix for app code, which is usually slow because of DOM and framework work, not raw computation.

## Framework-level levers

- **React:** avoid unnecessary renders (structure, memoisation or the React Compiler), use transitions or `useDeferredValue` for expensive non-urgent updates, and virtualise long lists. Concurrency cannot split one slow component or a huge commit.
- **Event handlers on scroll, resize and input:** throttle visual updates with `requestAnimationFrame`, debounce expensive side effects, and use passive listeners for touch and wheel so scrolling does not wait for JavaScript.
- **Third-party scripts:** frequently the biggest source of long tasks. Load them after interaction, behind facades, or not at all.

parts.label: Virtualisation and memory
parts.body:
## Virtualisation: render only what is visible

A table with 10,000 rows of 8 cells is 80,000+ DOM nodes. Creating them costs JavaScript and layout time; keeping them costs memory and makes every style recalculation slower; and in React, any update to the list touches all of them. **Virtualisation** (also called windowing) renders only the rows in or near the viewport, plus a small **overscan** buffer, inside a container whose total height matches the full list so the scrollbar behaves normally.

```text
scroll container (height 600px, overflow: auto)
  inner spacer (height = 10,000 rows x 40px = 400,000px)
    rows 120..140 absolutely positioned (or translated) at top = index x 40px
    overscan: rows 115..119 and 141..145 also rendered
on scroll: compute first = floor(scrollTop / rowHeight), render [first - overscan, first + visible + overscan]
```

Libraries: **TanStack Virtual** (headless, works with any markup, supports dynamic measurement, horizontal and grid layouts) and **react-window** (smaller, simpler); web.dev's "Virtualize large lists with react-window" walks through the latter.

### The hard parts

| Problem | Why | Approach |
|---|---|---|
| Variable row heights | Offsets cannot be computed by multiplication | Estimate sizes, measure rendered rows (`ResizeObserver`), keep a prefix-sum of offsets, correct as rows are measured |
| Scroll jumping when measured heights differ from estimates | Content above the viewport changes size | Adjust `scrollTop` by the delta for rows above the viewport (scroll anchoring) |
| Fast scrolling shows blank areas | Rendering cannot keep up | Larger overscan, cheaper rows (memoised, no heavy effects), placeholders |
| Find-in-page (Ctrl+F) cannot find off-screen rows | They are not in the DOM | Provide in-app search; or consider `content-visibility: auto` instead, which keeps nodes in the DOM |
| Accessibility | Screen readers see only rendered rows | Use `aria-rowcount` / `aria-rowindex` on grids, or `aria-setsize` / `aria-posinset` on list items; keep focus on a real element when rows recycle |
| Keyboard focus lost when the focused row scrolls out | Its node is unmounted | Keep the focused row rendered, or manage focus with `aria-activedescendant` |
| Infinite loading | Data arrives in pages | Combine with a sentinel row and fetching the next page when near the end |

### Virtualise or not?

- **Hundreds of simple rows:** often fine without virtualisation; try `content-visibility: auto` first, which keeps native find-in-page and accessibility.
- **Thousands of rows or complex cells:** virtualise.
- **Data grids (spreadsheet-like):** virtualise both rows and columns, and keep cell components very cheap.
- **Pagination** is a legitimate alternative, especially for search results, and is better for SEO and shareable URLs.

## Memory leaks in single-page apps

A memory leak in JavaScript is memory that is **still reachable** from a root (the global object, the DOM, an active closure, a pending timer) although the app no longer needs it, so the garbage collector cannot reclaim it. Leaks barely matter on a page that reloads often; they matter in long-lived SPAs (dashboards, email clients, editors) where memory grows over hours until the tab becomes sluggish or crashes. Growing memory also increases garbage collection time, which shows up as jank.

### The usual suspects

1. **Global event listeners not removed:** `window.addEventListener('resize', handler)` in a component without cleanup. Each mount adds another handler that closes over the component's state and DOM.
2. **Detached DOM trees:** nodes removed from the document but still referenced from JavaScript (a cache, an array of "previous elements", a closure in a third-party widget). The whole subtree stays alive.
3. **Timers and intervals** never cleared, closing over large data.
4. **Subscriptions:** WebSockets, store subscriptions, `IntersectionObserver` and `ResizeObserver` instances never disconnected.
5. **Unbounded caches:** a `Map` keyed by request URL or object that grows forever. Use an LRU with a size limit, or `WeakMap` when entries should die with their keys.
6. **Closures capturing more than needed:** a small callback that references a large array keeps the array alive as long as the callback lives.
7. **Console logging objects in production:** DevTools keeps logged objects reachable when it is open.

In React, the pattern is consistent: **every effect that subscribes must return a cleanup function**, and Strict Mode's mount-unmount-mount in development exists to surface missing cleanups. `AbortController` is a convenient single handle to remove multiple listeners and cancel fetches at once.

### Finding a leak with DevTools

Chrome DevTools' "Fix memory problems" guide describes the workflow:

1. **Confirm growth.** Use the Performance panel with the Memory checkbox, or the Performance Monitor, and repeat an action (open and close a modal 10 times). A sawtooth that returns to baseline after GC is healthy; a staircase that keeps rising is a leak. Use the "collect garbage" button before measuring.
2. **Heap snapshot comparison.** In the Memory panel take a snapshot, perform the action several times, take another, and use the **Comparison** view sorted by size delta or the "Objects allocated between snapshots" filter.
3. **Look for detached elements.** Filter for "Detached" to find DOM nodes no longer in the document but still retained. Recent Chrome versions also offer a dedicated detached-elements view.
4. **Follow the retainers.** Select an object; the Retainers pane shows the reference chain to a GC root, for example `Window -> listeners -> resize -> closure -> ChartComponent -> canvas`. That chain names the code to fix.
5. **Allocation timeline** (allocation instrumentation on timeline) shows what was allocated when, useful for finding which action creates objects that never die.
6. **Verify the fix** by repeating the comparison: the delta should be near zero.

For production signals, `performance.measureUserAgentSpecificMemory()` reports memory use in cross-origin-isolated pages in Chromium, which some teams sample to catch regressions across releases.

parts.label: Profiling and interview
parts.body:
## Profiling in Chrome DevTools, step by step

Guessing at runtime performance wastes days. A trace shows exactly where the time went. The Chrome DevTools "Analyze runtime performance" guide is the reference; here is the workflow that works in practice.

### 1. Set up a realistic environment

- Use an **incognito window** or a clean profile so extensions do not add scripts.
- Profile a **production build**. Development builds of React and other frameworks do extra work (warnings, Strict Mode double renders) and are much slower.
- Enable **CPU throttling** (4x or 6x, or a calibrated preset for a mid-range phone) in the Performance panel. Your laptop is several times faster than your median user's phone.
- For loading issues also apply network throttling; for interaction issues it matters less.

### 2. Record the right thing

- For an interaction: start recording, perform the slow interaction once or twice, stop. Keep recordings short (a few seconds) so they are readable.
- For load: use the reload-and-record button.
- The panel's live metrics view shows local LCP, CLS and INP as you interact, with each interaction listed and its phases (input delay, processing, presentation), plus field data from CrUX for comparison when available.

### 3. Read the trace from the top down

| Track | What to look for |
|---|---|
| Interactions | Each interaction with its duration; long ones are flagged. Click to select the time range |
| Frames | Dropped or partially presented frames during animations and scrolling |
| Main | The flame chart. Grey task bars; long tasks have a red corner and red hatching beyond 50 ms |
| Timings | FCP, LCP, DCL markers, and your own `performance.mark` / `measure` calls |
| Layout shifts | Which elements moved, when |
| Network | Request waterfall, priorities, render-blocking flags |
| Custom tracks | React 19.2 adds Scheduler and Components tracks showing priorities and component render times |

In the **Main** flame chart, the x-axis is time and the y-axis is call stack depth. Colours mark activity type: yellow for scripting, purple for style and layout, green for paint and compositing. Wide yellow blocks are JavaScript; wide purple blocks are rendering work, often caused by your JavaScript.

### 4. Drill into a long task

1. Click the long task. The **Summary** tab shows the split between scripting, rendering and painting.
2. **Bottom-Up** sorts functions by self time: the functions that actually burned CPU, regardless of who called them. Start here to find hot spots (a JSON parse, a regex, a sort, a framework's reconcile function).
3. **Call Tree** shows the top-down hierarchy: which entry point (an event handler, a timer) led to the cost.
4. **Event Log** lists activities in order.
5. Purple "Recalculate Style" or "Layout" blocks inside your function with a **"Forced reflow"** warning point to layout thrashing; the warning links to the line that read layout.
6. Hover a task for the "Long task" annotation and check the **Insights** sidebar, which surfaces common problems (forced reflow, large DOM, third parties, render-blocking requests) with links to the relevant events.

### 5. Connect to framework-level cause

The browser trace shows *that* React's reconcile functions took 180 ms; the **React DevTools Profiler** shows *which components* rendered and *why*. Use both: Performance panel for the shape of the problem, React Profiler for the component-level fix.

### 6. Add your own markers

`performance.mark('filter-start')` and `performance.measure('filter', 'filter-start')` appear in the Timings track, and the same entries can be sent to RUM. User Timing is the cheapest way to make your own code readable in traces and measurable in the field.

### Memory and other panels

- **Memory panel:** heap snapshots, allocation timeline, allocation sampling (see the leaks section).
- **Performance Monitor:** live CPU usage, JS heap size, DOM node count, layouts and style recalcs per second. A DOM node count that only grows is a leak signal.
- **Rendering drawer:** paint flashing, layout shift regions, layer borders, frame rendering stats. Useful for spotting areas that repaint on every scroll.
- **Layers panel:** which elements are composited and why, and their memory cost.

## What interviewers are really testing

Runtime performance questions check whether you understand the single main thread, can find the cause of jank with tools instead of guesses, and know the menu of fixes and their trade-offs: do less, yield, schedule, move to a worker, render less (virtualise), avoid layout thrash, and stop leaks. Senior candidates are expected to describe a real debugging story with numbers.

## Question 1: "What is a long task and why does it matter?"

**Model answer:** Any main-thread task longer than 50 ms. While it runs, the browser cannot handle input or render frames, so a tap during it waits; that waiting is INP input delay, and long tasks during handlers are INP processing time. The 50 ms comes from the RAIL model's goal of responding within 100 ms. In the lab I see them in the Performance panel and as TBT; in the field I use the Long Animation Frames API, which also attributes slow frames to specific scripts.

## Question 2: "How do you break up a long task?"

**Model answer:** First check whether the work is needed at all or can be cached. If not, chunk it and yield between chunks with a time budget of 5 to 10 ms: `scheduler.yield()` where available, which resumes at the front of the queue, otherwise `setTimeout`. For interactions, update the UI first, yield so the frame paints, then do the rest. Work that does not need the DOM, like parsing or filtering a large dataset, goes to a Web Worker. Background work can use `scheduler.postTask` with background priority or `requestIdleCallback` with a timeout.

## Question 3: "A data table with 20,000 rows is janky when scrolling and filtering. Fix it."

**Model answer, structured:**

1. **Profile** with CPU throttling: likely huge DOM, long style and layout, and React re-rendering every row on filter.
2. **Virtualise** rows (and columns if wide) with overscan, keeping row components cheap and memoised; handle accessibility with `aria-rowcount` and `aria-rowindex`.
3. **Filtering:** keep the input urgent, compute results in a transition or deferred value, and move heavy filtering or sorting to a worker with a precomputed index.
4. **Scrolling:** passive listeners, no layout reads in scroll handlers, sticky headers with CSS rather than JavaScript.
5. **Verify** frame rate and interaction durations in a new trace, then watch field INP for that page.

## Question 4: "How do you find and fix a memory leak in an SPA?"

**Model answer:** Reproduce with a repeatable action and confirm a staircase in memory after forced GC. Take heap snapshots before and after repeating the action and compare; look for detached DOM nodes and growing arrays or maps. Follow the retainer chain to the root, typically a global listener, an uncleared interval, a store subscription or an unbounded cache. Fix with effect cleanups, `AbortController` for listeners and fetches, disconnecting observers, `WeakMap` or a bounded LRU for caches. Then repeat the comparison to confirm the delta is flat.

## Question 5: "When would you use a Web Worker, and what are the costs?"

**Model answer:** For CPU-heavy, DOM-free work: parsing, search, diffing, image and data processing. Costs: structured cloning of messages, which is itself main-thread work for large objects, so transfer `ArrayBuffer`s or keep data in the worker; no DOM access; more complex code, eased with Comlink; and worker startup time. It does not help when the cost is rendering a huge DOM.

## Quick-fire follow-ups

| Follow-up | Strong short answer |
|---|---|
| "Why profile with CPU throttling?" | Developer laptops are several times faster than median user devices |
| "Why profile production builds?" | Dev builds add checks and double renders, distorting results |
| "Bottom-Up vs Call Tree?" | Bottom-Up ranks self time (hot functions); Call Tree shows the entry point path |
| "What does a Forced reflow warning mean?" | A layout read after a write forced synchronous layout inside your script |
| "content-visibility vs virtualisation?" | `content-visibility` keeps nodes in the DOM but skips rendering off-screen; virtualisation removes them; the latter scales further |
| "Why passive listeners?" | The compositor need not wait for JavaScript before scrolling |
| "What is LoAF?" | Long Animation Frames API: slow frames with script attribution, for field diagnosis |

## Common mistakes

- Profiling on a fast laptop without throttling and concluding "it is fine".
- Reaching for `useMemo` everywhere before finding the actual hot spot.
- Chunking work with `requestIdleCallback` for user-visible results, which may never run on a busy page.
- Virtualising without handling focus, keyboard navigation and screen reader counts.
- Forgetting third-party scripts, which LoAF attribution often reveals as the real culprit.
- Calling growing memory "a leak" without checking whether it drops after garbage collection.

flowchart TD
  Start["Janky interaction reported"] --> Rec["Record in Performance panel: prod build, 4x CPU throttle"]
  Rec --> LT{"Long task under the interaction?"}
  LT -->|"mostly yellow scripting"| BU["Bottom-Up: hottest functions by self time"]
  LT -->|"mostly purple rendering work"| FR{"Forced reflow warning?"}
  FR -->|"yes"| Batch["Batch reads before writes, use observers"]
  FR -->|"no"| DOM["Shrink DOM: virtualise, content-visibility, containment"]
  BU --> Who{"Whose code?"}
  Who -->|"framework render"| RP["React Profiler: which components and why"]
  Who -->|"app logic"| Split["Cache, chunk and yield, or move to a worker"]
  Who -->|"third party"| TP["Defer, facade or remove the script"]

keyPoints: The main thread runs JavaScript, style, layout, paint and event dispatch one task at a time; tasks over 50 ms are long tasks that delay input and frames.
Long Animation Frames attributes slow frames to scripts in the field; TBT is the lab proxy during load.
Break up unavoidable work with a time budget and scheduler.yield (fallback setTimeout); paint interaction feedback first, then do the rest.
Rendering cost scales with DOM size and invalidation scope: avoid forced synchronous layout, use containment, content-visibility and compositor-only animations.
Web Workers suit CPU-heavy DOM-free work; structured cloning has a cost, so transfer buffers or keep data in the worker.
Virtualise thousands of rows, handling variable heights, focus and screen reader counts; content-visibility is a lighter option for moderate lists.
Leaks are reachable-but-unneeded memory: global listeners, detached DOM, timers, subscriptions, unbounded caches. Find them with heap snapshot comparison and retainers.

check.q: A click handler updates a button, then synchronously saves to IndexedDB, recomputes stats and sends analytics, taking 220 ms total. What change most directly improves INP?
options: Wrap the handler in useMemo
Update the button, yield to the main thread so the frame paints, then run the remaining work
Add more overscan to the list
Move the button into an iframe
check.why: INP ends at the next paint after the interaction. Painting the visual feedback first and deferring non-visual work after a yield removes it from the interaction's processing time.

check.q: Memory rises in a staircase each time a modal is opened and closed, even after forcing garbage collection. Heap snapshots show detached div trees retained by a closure. What is the most likely cause?
options: The browser's garbage collector is disabled in production
Too many CSS rules
A listener or subscription registered by the modal is never removed, keeping its closure and DOM alive
The modal uses transform animations
check.why: Detached DOM retained by a closure is the classic signature of a global listener, timer or subscription without cleanup. The retainer chain in the snapshot points to the exact registration.

check.q: Which statement about virtualising a 20,000-row list is accurate?
options: It keeps DOM size roughly proportional to the visible rows, but needs extra work for focus, find-in-page and screen reader row counts
It makes every row available to the browser's find-in-page
It removes the need for stable keys or memoised rows
It is unnecessary because React's virtual DOM already avoids creating DOM nodes
check.why: Only visible rows plus overscan are mounted, which bounds DOM and render cost. Off-screen rows do not exist in the DOM, so find-in-page, focus and assistive technology need explicit handling.
